title: Least squares with QR
objectives: Factor $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ and see why it makes least squares stable.

screens.title: Straighten the columns
screens.prose: Gram-Schmidt turns the columns $\mathbf{a}_1$, $\mathbf{a}_2$ of $\mathbf{A}$ into orthonormal $\mathbf{q}_1$, $\mathbf{q}_2$, the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$. Start with the first column.
screens.question: Find $\mathbf{q}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 / |\mathbf{a}_1|$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each entry of $(1, 2, 2)$ by its length.

byKey.r0c1: The length is $\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$, not $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$. So the first entry is $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

explain.text: $|\mathbf{a}_1| = 3$, so $\mathbf{q}_1 = (\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3})$. The 3 we divided by is worth keeping: $\mathbf{a}_1 = 3\mathbf{q}_1$.

screens.prose: For $\mathbf{q}_2$, remove the part of $\mathbf{a}_2 = (3, 3, 0)$ along $\mathbf{q}_1$: $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{a}_2 - (\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_2)\,\mathbf{q}_1$. Then divide $\mathbf{v}$ by its length.
screens.question: Find $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_2 = 3$, subtract $3\mathbf{q}_1 = (1, 2, 2)$ from $\mathbf{a}_2$, then normalise.

explain.text: $\mathbf{v} = (2, 1, -2)$, and $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}(2 + 2 - 4) = 0$. Both numbers are worth keeping: $\mathbf{a}_2 = 3\mathbf{q}_1 + 3\mathbf{q}_2$.

screens.title: The matrix R
screens.prose: The recipe is $\mathbf{a}_1 = 3\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = 3\mathbf{q}_1 + 3\mathbf{q}_2$. Collect the numbers in a matrix $\mathbf{R}$, so that $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$. Since $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$, multiplying by $\mathbf{Q}^T$ gives $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$.
screens.question: Compute $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$.

hints.text: Row 2, column 1 is $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{a}_1$. How was $\mathbf{q}_2$ built?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each row of $\mathbf{Q}^T$ with each column of $\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{R}$ holds the numbers from Gram-Schmidt: lengths on the diagonal, removed amounts above it. The 0 below the diagonal is no accident, because $\mathbf{q}_2$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}_1$. This is the factorisation $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$.

screens.prose: With three columns, $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$ is 3 × 3. Entry $(i, j)$ is $\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}_j$. Remember that $\mathbf{a}_j$ is built from $\mathbf{q}_1$ up to $\mathbf{q}_j$ only.
screens.question: Tap every entry that Gram-Schmidt forces to be 0.

hints.text: $\mathbf{q}_3$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$, and so to $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$.
An entry is 0 when $i > j$: the $\mathbf{q}$ comes later than the $\mathbf{a}$.

feedback.correct: The three entries below the diagonal are 0, so $\mathbf{R}$ is upper triangular.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the entries where the q comes later than the a.

byKey.upper: You tapped the entries above the diagonal. There $\mathbf{q}_i$ comes before $\mathbf{a}_j$, which contains it, so they are not 0.
byKey.R-1-1: Diagonal entries are the lengths from Gram-Schmidt. They are positive.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a}_j$ lies in the span of $\mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_j$, and each later $\mathbf{q}_i$ is perpendicular to all of those. So $\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}_j = 0$ whenever $i > j$. That is why $\mathbf{R}$ is always upper triangular.

screens.title: Least squares with Q and R
screens.prose: Now fit $\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} \approx \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} = (2, 1, 7)$. With $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ the normal equations become $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$, as we will prove. First the right-hand side.
screens.question: Compute $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each row of $\mathbf{Q}^T$ with $\mathbf{b} = (2, 1, 7)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b} = (6, -3)$ holds the components of $\mathbf{b}$ along $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$. So the projection is $\mathbf{p} = 6\mathbf{q}_1 - 3\mathbf{q}_2 = (0, 3, 6)$.

screens.prose: Solve $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$. $\mathbf{R}$ is triangular, so start from the bottom row: **back substitution**.
screens.question: Find $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

hints.text: So $\hat{x}_2 = -1$. Put it into the top row: $3\hat{x}_1 + 3(-1) = 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve the bottom row first, then put $\hat{x}_2$ into the top row.

byKey.r0c1: Use $\hat{x}_2 = -1$ in the top row: $3\hat{x}_1 - 3 = 6$, so $\hat{x}_1 = 3$.

explain.text: $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (3, -1)$ and $\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (0, 3, 6)$, the projection. Check with the normal equations: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (9 \cdot 3 - 9,\ 9 \cdot 3 - 18) = (18, 9) = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$.

screens.prose: Three classmates computed $\mathbf{R}$ for the same $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$, and got different answers.
screens.question: Which is $\mathbf{R}$?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{R}^T = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{Q}$. You multiplied in the wrong order: $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$.
That is $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}^T$, a 3 × 3 matrix. $\mathbf{R}$ must be 2 × 2: $\mathbf{Q}^T$ (2 × 3) times $\mathbf{A}$ (3 × 2).
A non-zero entry below the diagonal would mean $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{a}_1 \neq 0$. Gram-Schmidt makes it 0.

hints.text: Check the shape first, then the entry below the diagonal.

feedback.correct: 2 × 2 and upper triangular, as $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$ must be.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$ is 2 × 2 with a 0 below the diagonal.

byKey.aqt: You computed $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}^T$. The order matters: $\mathbf{Q}^T$ goes on the left, so that $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ cancels in $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$.
byKey.lower: Yours is lower triangular: you formed $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{Q}$, the transpose of $\mathbf{R}$.

explain.text: From $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$, multiply on the left by $\mathbf{Q}^T$: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}$. On the right there is nothing to cancel, since $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ is a projection, not $\mathbf{I}$.

screens.prose: Why does $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$ solve least squares? Start from the normal equations, which come from the error being perpendicular to $C(\mathbf{A})$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$, multiplying by $(\mathbf{R}^T)^{-1}$, which exists as $\mathbf{R}$ is triangular with a non-zero diagonal

hints.text: Start from the equations you already trust.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is never formed: only $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$ are needed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$ and substitute $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$.

byKey.r3: Cancelling $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ needs it written out first, after substituting.
byKey.r4: Removing $\mathbf{R}^T$ is the last step, once both sides start with it.

explain.text: The diagonal of $\mathbf{R}$ holds the lengths from Gram-Schmidt, which are positive when the columns are independent. So $\mathbf{R}^T$ can be cancelled, leaving a triangular system. Back substitution then solves it one unknown at a time.

screens.title: Why not form AᵀA
screens.prose: Two nearly parallel columns: $\mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (1, 1.01, 0.99)$. Their difference shows up in the second decimal place of $\mathbf{A}$, but only in the fourth of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.
screens.question: A calculator keeps 4 significant figures, so it stores 3.0002 as 3.000. What is $\det(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})$ as stored?

feedback.correct: The stored $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is singular: the normal equations have lost the second column.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round 3.0002 to 3.000 first, then take the determinant.

byKey.exact: 0.0006 is the exact determinant, $9.0006 - 9$. After rounding the 0.0002 is gone, and so is the determinant.
byKey.nine: That is one product. The determinant subtracts the other: $9 - 9$.

explain.text: Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the small difference $0.01$ into $0.0002$. The condition number goes from about 245 for $\mathbf{A}$ to about 60,000 for $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$: it is squared. QR keeps it at $\mathbf{A}$'s size: $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.732 & 1.732 \\ 0 & 0.0141 \end{pmatrix}$ holds the difference at $\sqrt{2} \times 0.01$.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def ls_qr(A, b):
    A = np.array(A, dtype=float)
    b = np.array(b, dtype=float)
    Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A)   # reduced: Q is m x n
    rhs = Q.T @ b            # Q^T b
    x_hat = np.linalg.solve(R, rhs)  # solve R x = rhs
    return x_hat

explain.text:
NumPy's reduced QR gives a 3 × 2 `Q` and a 2 × 2 `R`, possibly with negative signs on the diagonal. Signs cancel between `Q` and `R`, so $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is the same.

```python
rhs = Q.T @ b                     # components along q1, q2
x_hat = np.linalg.solve(R, rhs)   # triangular solve
```

ideas: Gram-Schmidt turns the columns of $\mathbf{A}$ into $\mathbf{Q}$. $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$ records the recipe and is upper triangular.
The normal equations become $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$, solved by back substitution from the bottom row.
Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the condition number. QR works on $\mathbf{A}$ directly, which is why software prefers it.

formula.name: Least squares by QR
formula.note: $\mathbf{R}$ is square and upper triangular, with the Gram-Schmidt lengths on its diagonal.

summary.trap: $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$, not $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}^T$. A non-zero entry below its diagonal means an arithmetic slip.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ is 5 × 3 with independent columns, and $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ with $\mathbf{Q}$ 5 × 3.
quiz.question: What shape is $\mathbf{R}$?

options.why: That is the shape of $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$. $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$ is (3 × 5)(5 × 3).
That is the shape of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$. $\mathbf{R}$ has one row per column of $\mathbf{Q}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$ is 3 × 3: one row and one column per column of $\mathbf{A}$. It is upper triangular with positive diagonal.

quiz.question: What is $\hat{x}_1$?

quiz.prose: A design matrix $\mathbf{A}$ has condition number about 1,000.
quiz.question: About what is the condition number of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$?

options.why: That is what QR works with. Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares it.
The condition number is multiplied by itself, not doubled.
That is the square root. $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ makes things worse, not better.

feedback.correct: $1000^2 = 10^6$: about six digits of accuracy lost instead of three.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the condition number.

explain.text: $\kappa(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}) = \kappa(\mathbf{A})^2 = 10^6$. Roughly, you lose about $\log_{10}\kappa$ digits, so six instead of three. That is why QR, or the SVD, is used.
